newsitem.title: UK: Dollar/yen pummelled in Europe by Japan rate fears.
newsitem.headline: Dollar/yen pummelled in Europe by Japan rate fears.

text.p: The dollar ended almost two full yen lower in Europe on Thursday and extended its decline this month to almost 10 percent as heightened speculation of a rise in Japanese interest rates sent ripples through global currency markets, said analysts.

The prospect of a rise in Japanese rates is prompting investors who extensively used cheap yen borrowings to fund high-yield, high-risk currency positions around the world --so called carry trades -- to pare back their riskier investments.
As a result, the yen rally has coincided with severe selling pressure on currencies like the Thai baht and Czech crown.

"At the end of the day, what we're seeing is a sharp rethink of carry trades in risk markets which has been triggered by the sudden shift in Japanese interest rate expectations," said Joe Prendergast, foreign exchange strategist at Merrill Lynch.
"The collapse in dollar/yen itself has been exaggerated by the argument both Japan and the U.S. have engineered a stronger yen to offset the pressures that are building for a rate rise."

The dollar slumped to as low as 114.70 yen in early trade from 117.95/05 late Wednesday and although it recovered some lost ground through the session it still ended sharply down at 116.23/33 at 1520 GMT.

The dollar also weakened briefly against the mark but the extent to which the day's move was concentrated in the yen was illustrated by a further steep decline in the mark/yen cross rate to a one-year low at 68.32.
Dollar/mark closed the day slightly higher at 1.6983/88 compared with 1.6969/79 late Wednesday.
The yen surge overnight was exaggerated by a rumour that U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin favoured the dollar settling back to about 115 yen.
Traders contacted could not source the story but volatile markets needed only the slightest excuse to buy yen.

The interest rate speculation was aggravated later when Koichi Kato, secretary-general of Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party, was quoted by Jiji news agency as saying Japan may face pressure to change its current low interest rates as it progresses with financial market deregulation.

Long-term Japanese interest rates have been rising in recent weeks and there is a concern that officials are preparing the market for a rise if the official discount rate. The discount rate has been as low as 0.50 percent since September 1995.
"There is a view in the market that we're going to get a rate hike in Japan," said Nigel Richardson, economist at Yamaichi

A belief that extra-tight European fiscal policy in the run-up to European monetary union offsets similar pressures for higher European interest rates has kept the mark and its satellite currencies subdued, traders said.

Moreover, there is still a degree of uncertainty about whether the U.S. Federal Reserve will lift interest rates at its policy-making meeting next week and the chance of another quarter-point rise in the Fed funds rate has buoyed dollar/mark.
The latest stream of economic data out of the U.S. today was a mixed bag, and while the numbers look benign, some say the Fed will raise rates as an insurance against inflation.

Talk of a rise of both Japanese and U.S. interest rates is proving to be a squeeze on international liquidity, however, and this has shaken peripheral markets like those of Thailand and the Czech Republic.

Analysts said there is little to connect the sudden drop in the baht and the crown apart from a belief that these units have benefited a lot from foreign investment and will suffer disproportionately from a retrenchment of global capital.
Large current account deficits dog both currencies and leave them highly vulnerable to foreign investment trends.
--Mike Dolan, London newsroom +44 171 542 6762
